successRegex: \nDecision traces for C-1042, the precedent this run reads\n
Debt to Income Limit: +(above|below) the line +\(
\nPrecedent trail, now that this decision is on file\n
\nTranscript for this run, from Spring AI chat memory\n

aiValidation.expectedBehavior: A Spring AI CallAdvisor puts one loan application for company C-1042 in front of the model and lets the model decide it. Java reads the company, its policies and its standing denials out of Neo4j and measures three named policies (Minimum Credit Score, Debt to Income Limit, Repeat Denial Escalation), then hands those measurements over as facts rather than as a verdict. One of three named underwriters is drawn at random per run and their disposition goes into the prompt. The model answers with a structured verdict, and only then is the decision written back to the graph as a decision trace. Validate that: (1) the 'Decision traces for C-1042' section lists at least one prior decision with a date, outcome and amount, showing the precedent for this run was read out of the graph rather than supplied in the prompt; (2) 'On duty for this run' names one underwriter with a title and years on the job, so a reader who sees two different answers to identical arguments can see who answered; (3) the 'Policies, as measured' block reports all three policies, each marked 'above the line' or 'below the line' with a numeric detail naming the observed value and the threshold, which is the bank's arithmetic and not the outcome; (4) the verdict line gives APPROVED or DENIED with a confidence of clear or borderline and a reason, and the 'line crossed' line beneath it either names a policy or says none. The verdict is NOT required to agree with the measurements, and a disagreement is the demo rather than a failure: a denial where everything measured above the line, and an approval that went past a line, are both correct outcomes, because the model is the underwriter and the thresholds are guidance it is allowed to weigh. What would be wrong is a 'line crossed' naming a policy that measured above the line, or naming a policy that appears nowhere in the block; (5) the paragraph that follows explains that same verdict in the voice of a letter to the applicant, without inventing a different outcome, a different deciding policy, or figures that appear nowhere in the block; (6) the 'Precedent trail' block walks each denial on file out to the policy that decided it, the exception that set it aside if there is one, and the later decisions it has since driven, with 'none' and 'nothing yet' being correct answers rather than failures; (7) 'Which underwriter approves past which line' either lists underwriter and policy pairs with counts or says nobody has been approved past a line yet, and both are correct; (8) 'Who has set aside whose denial' either lists one row per exception granted, naming who granted it, the decision it was granted against, and who decided that denial, or says nobody has set aside a denial yet, and both are correct: the model may independently judge that an older standing denial should stop counting as precedent, separately from today's outcome, but is not required to on any given run, and 'exception' appearing under the verdict as a decisionId being set aside with a justification is likewise optional, not a requirement of a correct run; (9) the 'Transcript for this run, from Spring AI chat memory' section shows a USER question about C-1042 and a non-empty ASSISTANT turn carrying that same explanation as prose rather than as JSON, showing the exchange was persisted to Spring AI chat memory and the structured verdict never reached it. Which policy is below the line is NOT fixed and must not be treated as a failure either way: a fresh graph has Debt to Income Limit below the line, while a graph already holding two or more standing denials for C-1042 inside the rolling window has Repeat Denial Escalation below it as well, because each run's own decision becomes precedent for the next. The underwriter who draws the run, the outcome on a borderline file, the seeded history dates and the model's exact wording all vary between runs, so none of them should be matched literally.
